warmup.q: You schedule a health check with scheduleAtFixedRate(check, 0, 10, SECONDS). On its fifth run, the ledger ping inside it throws an IllegalStateException that nothing catches. What happens next?
options: The exception is logged and the check runs again 10 seconds later
The scheduler thread dies, a new one starts, and the check carries on
The check never runs again, and nothing is logged
warmup.why: The Javadoc says that if any execution throws, "subsequent executions are suppressed". The exception is stored in the ScheduledFuture and nothing prints it. The scheduler itself is fine and keeps running its other tasks, which is why the failure is so easy to miss.

sections.h: Three ways to schedule work, and which jobs belong elsewhere
sections.html:
Before JDK 5, the JDK's scheduler was java.util.Timer, and it has a trap. It runs every task on one thread, and if one task throws, that thread dies and the whole Timer is cancelled: every other task on it stops too, and the next schedule call throws IllegalStateException. So skip Timer. JDK 5 replaced it with the ScheduledExecutorService interface and its implementation, ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor.

A ScheduledExecutorService runs tasks later, or over and over. You get one from Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(n) or newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(), and three of its methods do nearly all the work:

Java
ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2);

scheduler.schedule(this::expireHold, 15, TimeUnit.MINUTES);                     // once, after a delay
scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::sendHeartbeat, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);    // on a timetable
scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshFxRate, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);  // with a gap between runs
Kotlin
val scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2)

scheduler.schedule(this::expireHold, 15, TimeUnit.MINUTES)                     // once, after a delay
scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::sendHeartbeat, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)    // on a timetable
scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshFxRate, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)  // with a gap between runs

Each call returns a ScheduledFuture, a Future that also knows its remaining delay. Cancel it to stop a periodic task. For a periodic task, get() never returns normally: it waits until the task is cancelled or fails. The scheduler is a pool like any other, so shut it down, or its threads keep the JVM alive.

Some schedules don't belong in the JVM at all. An in-process scheduler forgets everything when the pod restarts, and with three replicas every job runs three times. The settlement export each night, a monthly fee run, anything with business meaning: put those in a cron job, a scheduler with a database such as Quartz, or a Temporal schedule. The JVM scheduler is for in-process housekeeping, like refreshing a cache, sending heartbeats or expiring holds kept in memory.

try.title: Pick the method
steps: For each job, choose schedule, scheduleAtFixedRate, scheduleWithFixedDelay, or "not in the JVM": (a) drop an idempotency key from an in-memory cache 10 minutes after it was stored; (b) send the issuer a heartbeat every 30 seconds, which it expects on a steady beat; (c) refresh FX rates from a provider whose calls sometimes take 20 seconds; (d) export the settlement file once a night.
Write one sentence of reasoning for each before you read the answer.
try.expect: (a) schedule: it is a one-shot delay. (b) Fixed rate: the timing is the point. (c) Fixed delay: a slow call pushes the next one later instead of causing a burst of catch-up calls. (d) Not in the JVM: a restart loses the schedule and every replica would export the file.

sections.h: Fixed rate catches up, fixed delay never does
sections.html:
The two periodic methods measure the period from different places.

scheduleAtFixedRate(task, initialDelay, period, unit) follows a timetable fixed in advance. Runs are due at initialDelay, then initialDelay + period, then initialDelay + 2 x period, and so on. scheduleWithFixedDelay(task, initialDelay, delay, unit) waits delay after each run ends, then starts the next one.

While runs are short, you can't tell them apart. They split when one run is slow. Take a 100 ms period where the second run takes 250 ms and the others 10 ms. In the lab's model, which counts virtual milliseconds, the runs start at:

fixed rate:   0, 100, 350, 360, 400, 500, 600
fixed delay:  0, 110, 460, 570, 680, 790, 900

RateVsDelayDemo shows the same shape with a few milliseconds of real-world noise.

Both rows follow from what the executor does after each run. It puts a periodic task back in its queue only when the run returns, with a new due time. For fixed rate the new due time is the old due time plus the period. For fixed delay it is the current time plus the delay. A due time that is already in the past means "run as soon as a thread is free".

Fixed rate never runs two executions at once. A late run starts as soon as the previous one ends, and then the overdue runs go back to back (runs 3 and 4 above) until the schedule is back on its timetable. By run 5 it is on time again. Fixed delay has no timetable to catch up with, so a slow run just pushes everything after it later.

Pick fixed rate when the timing itself is the point: a heartbeat the issuer expects every 30 seconds, a metrics flush per interval. Pick fixed delay when the task calls something that can slow down, like an FX provider or a database, because you never want a provider that just recovered to be hit with a burst of catch-up calls. For most housekeeping in a service, fixed delay is the safer default.

Neither method ever runs a task concurrently with itself, even on a scheduler with many threads. A task that takes 3 minutes on a 1 minute rate doesn't pile up three copies. It just runs late, every time.

try.title: Watch a slow run
steps: Run RateVsDelayDemo and compare its start times with the fixed-rate row above.
Run it again with -Pargs=delay. Before you do, predict when run 3 starts.

code.title: RateVsDelayDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l05; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** A 100 ms schedule whose second run takes 250 ms. Default: fixed rate. Pass "delay" for fixed delay. */ public class RateVsDelayDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean delay = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("delay"); ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(); AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger(); CountDownLatch sevenRuns = new CountDownLatch(7); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); Runnable sync = () -> { int n = runs.incrementAndGet(); long start = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; long work = n == 2 ? 250 : 10; // run 2 hits a slow ledger try { Thread.sleep(work); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } System.out.printf("run %d started at %4d ms, took %3d ms%n", n, start, work); sevenRuns.countDown(); }; ScheduledFuture<?> f = delay ? scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(sync, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) : scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(sync, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); System.out.println(delay ? "scheduleWithFixedDelay, 100 ms" : "scheduleAtFixedRate, 100 ms"); sevenRuns.await(); f.cancel(false); scheduler.shutdown(); } }

Default: fixed rate. Pass "delay" for fixed delay. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val delay = args.firstOrNull() == "delay" val scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor() val runs = AtomicInteger() val sevenRuns = CountDownLatch(7) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val sync = Runnable { val n = runs.incrementAndGet() val start = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val work = if (n == 2) 250L else 10L // run 2 hits a slow ledger try { Thread.sleep(work) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } println("run %d started at %4d ms, took %3d ms".format(n, start, work)) sevenRuns.countDown() } val f = if (delay) scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(sync, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) else scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(sync, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) println(if (delay) "scheduleWithFixedDelay, 100 ms" else "scheduleAtFixedRate, 100 ms") sevenRuns.await() f.cancel(false) scheduler.shutdown() }

try.expect: With fixed rate, runs 3 and 4 start within about 10 ms of each other, right after the slow run, and runs 5 to 7 are back on the 100 ms grid. With fixed delay, run 3 starts about 100 ms after run 2 ends (around 460 to 500 ms), and every later run is 110 ms after the one before. On a busy machine, all times drift a little later.

sections.h: One exception, and the schedule stops without a word
sections.html:
This sentence in the ScheduledExecutorService Javadoc causes more production surprises than any other in the package. A periodic task keeps running until it is cancelled, the executor terminates, or "an execution of the task throws an exception", and then: "Subsequent executions are suppressed."

Nothing is logged. The re-queue step from the previous section happens only when a run returns normally. A run that throws leaves its exception in the ScheduledFuture, the same way submit hides exceptions, and the task never goes back in the queue. Almost nobody calls get() on a periodic task's future. Here is SilentDeathDemo, a health check every 100 ms that throws on its third run:

health check 1
health check 2
health check 3
after 1 s: runs=3 isDone=true
get() threw ExecutionException, cause: java.lang.IllegalStateException: ledger ping timed out

Ten periods passed and three runs happened. In a real service, the FX rate quietly stops refreshing, a cache serves data that is days old, and the first sign is a customer complaint.

The fix is to catch inside the task, so that no exception ever reaches the scheduler:

Java
scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> {
    try {
        refreshFxRate();
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        log.warn("FX refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e);   // report it, keep the schedule
    }
}, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
Kotlin
scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay({
    try {
        refreshFxRate()
    } catch (e: RuntimeException) {
        log.warn("FX refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e)    // report it, keep the schedule
    }
}, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)

Catch RuntimeException (or Exception if the body calls checked-exception code), not Throwable. An OutOfMemoryError or a StackOverflowError means the JVM itself is in trouble, and a schedule that hides it will keep failing politely. Let errors stop the task and alert on them. The lab wraps the pattern once, as SafeTask.wrap, so every periodic task in a service gets it.

If you want to catch a dead schedule anyway, check future.isDone() from a health endpoint. For a periodic task that should run forever, done means dead.

try.title: Kill a schedule, then save it
steps: Run SilentDeathDemo. Count the health checks before the after 1 s line.
Run it with -Pargs=safe, which wraps the check in a try/catch. Predict the run count after one second.

code.title: SilentDeathDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** A health check every 100 ms that throws on its third run. Pass "safe" to catch inside the task. */ public class SilentDeathDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean safe = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("safe"); ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(); AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger(); Runnable check = () -> { int n = runs.incrementAndGet(); System.out.println("health check " + n); if (n == 3) throw new IllegalStateException("ledger ping timed out"); }; Runnable task = !safe ? check : () -> { try { check.run(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(" caught and logged: " + e.getMessage()); } }; ScheduledFuture<?> f = scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(task, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); Thread.sleep(1_000); // ten periods System.out.println("after 1 s: runs=" + runs.get() + " isDone=" + f.isDone()); if (f.isDone()) { try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: " + e.getCause()); } } scheduler.shutdownNow(); } }

alt.title: SilentDeathDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l05 import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** A health check every 100 ms that throws on its third run. Pass "safe" to catch inside the task. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val safe = args.firstOrNull() == "safe" val scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor() val runs = AtomicInteger() val check = Runnable { val n = runs.incrementAndGet() println("health check $n") if (n == 3) throw IllegalStateException("ledger ping timed out") } val task = if (!safe) check else Runnable { try { check.run() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println(" caught and logged: ${e.message}") } } val f = scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(task, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) Thread.sleep(1_000) // ten periods println("after 1 s: runs=${runs.get()} isDone=${f.isDone}") if (f.isDone) { try { f.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: ${e.cause}") } } scheduler.shutdownNow() }

try.expect: The first run prints three health checks and then nothing for the rest of the second: isDone=true, and get() reveals the exception. With safe, run 3 prints "caught and logged" and the checks continue to about 10 or 11 in the second, with isDone=false.

sections.h: ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor, and ForkJoinPool as a scheduler in JDK 25
sections.html:
newScheduledThreadPool(n) returns a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor: a ThreadPoolExecutor whose queue is ordered by due time. Its Javadoc says it "acts as a fixed-sized pool using corePoolSize threads and an unbounded queue", so the maximum pool size has no useful effect. That has three consequences worth knowing.

A scheduler with one thread runs one task at a time. A refresh that hangs for a minute delays every other task on that scheduler by a minute, heartbeats included. Give slow periodic work its own scheduler, or let the scheduled task only hand the real work to another pool.

Cancelled tasks stay in the queue until their due time by default. If you schedule and cancel a lot, for example one timeout per request, call setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true) so they don't pile up.

After shutdown(), one-shot delayed tasks still run when they come due, but periodic tasks stop. Those are the defaults of setExecuteExistingDelayedTasksAfterShutdownPolicy and setContinueExistingPeriodicTasksAfterShutdownPolicy, and they matter when a service shuts down with holds still waiting to expire.

JDK 25 adds a second scheduler you already have. ForkJoinPool now implements ScheduledExecutorService, so ForkJoinPool.commonPool() can schedule tasks too, with the same fixed-rate, fixed-delay and exception rules. It also gains submitWithTimeout, which cancels a task (or runs an action you pass) if it hasn't finished in time. This compiles only on JDK 25 or later, so it stays out of the labs:

Java
// JDK 25+
ForkJoinPool pool = ForkJoinPool.commonPool();
pool.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshFxRate, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
ForkJoinTask<Quote> quote = pool.submitWithTimeout(() -> fetchQuote(pair), 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, null);
// a null timeout action means: cancel(true) if it isn't done after 300 ms
Kotlin
// JDK 25+
val pool = ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
pool.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshFxRate, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
val quote: ForkJoinTask<Quote> = pool.submitWithTimeout({ fetchQuote(pair) }, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, null)
// a null timeout action means: cancel(true) if it isn't done after 300 ms

Keep blocking work off the common pool, scheduled or not. Every parallel stream and every default CompletableFuture in the JVM shares it, which lesson 8 of this track shows the hard way.

Check yourself: one single-thread scheduler runs a heartbeat at a 30-second fixed rate and an FX refresh with a 5-second fixed delay. A refresh starts just after a heartbeat and hangs for 90 seconds. How many heartbeats go out during the hang, and what happens when it ends? None go out during the hang, because the only thread is busy. When the refresh returns, the three heartbeats that came due in the meantime run back to back, because their due times are all in the past. The next refresh starts 5 seconds after the hung one ended.

analogy: Fixed rate is a train timetable. Trains are due at 8:00, 8:10, 8:20. If the 8:10 leaves twenty minutes late, the next train leaves as soon as the line is clear, and the one after that too, until they are back on the printed times. Fixed delay is a shuttle bus that leaves ten minutes after the previous one gets back, so a late bus just makes every later one later. The analogy breaks on parallel tracks. Two trains can run at once on a busy line. Two runs of the same scheduled task never overlap, however late they are.
world: Look for three schedules in a payment service. FX rates or BIN tables refreshed into memory: fixed delay, wrapped so a provider outage keeps the last good value, with the value's age exposed as a metric. A heartbeat or keep-alive to the issuer: fixed rate on its own scheduler, so a slow refresh can't delay it. In-memory expiry of authorization holds or idempotency keys: schedule per entry, or better, a cache with built-in expiry. Quarkus's @Scheduled is a different scheduler with its own rules (it has a concurrentExecution setting for overlapping runs), so check how it treats exceptions and overlap instead of assuming the JDK behavior carries over. Anything with business meaning, like the settlement export, belongs in a durable scheduler such as a Temporal schedule.
mistake: A periodic task with no try/catch. It works in every test, then one run throws (a 502 from the FX provider, a null in a response) and the schedule stops for good. The scheduler logs nothing, so the first sign is stale data hours later. People expect it to behave like a loop that logs and carries on. Wrap every periodic task body in a try/catch for RuntimeException that reports the failure, and expose isDone() or the age of the last success on a health endpoint.

compare.title: A fixed-delay refresher: scheduler vs coroutine loop

java.title: FxRefresh.java
java.html: ScheduledFuture<?> refresher = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { rate = fetchRate(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("FX refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e); } }, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // later refresher.cancel(false); // no more runs; a running fetch finishes

kotlin.title: FxRefresh.kt (kotlinx.coroutines)
kotlin.html: val refresher = scope.launch { while (isActive) { try { rate = fetchRate() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e // let cancellation through } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("FX refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e) } delay(5.seconds) // the gap is measured from the end of the run } } // later refresher.cancel() // stops at the next delay()

compare.note: Coroutines have no scheduler API. A loop with delay is a fixed-delay schedule, and a fixed rate needs you to compute the next due time yourself. The failure behavior differs in a useful way: an exception that escapes the JDK task disappears into the ScheduledFuture, while an exception that escapes launch propagates to the parent scope and its exception handler, so it is loud by default. Either way you catch inside the loop to keep it alive, and in Kotlin you rethrow CancellationException, or cancel() would be swallowed like any other exception.

worked.title: Why did the FX rate stop updating?

steps.say: Checkout prices in USD have used the same EUR/USD rate for six hours. The logs show no errors. Here is the refresher. Find the bug before reading on.
steps.code: scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate( () -> rate = fxProvider.eurUsd(), // throws on a 502 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

alt.html: scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate( { rate = fxProvider.eurUsd() }, // throws on a 502 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)

steps.say: Six hours ago the provider returned a 502 and eurUsd() threw. That run's exception went into the ScheduledFuture, which nobody holds, and every later run was suppressed. No log line, because nothing ever printed the exception. Fixed rate is a second, smaller problem: when the provider is slow, overdue runs fire back to back.
Catch inside the task, keep the last good rate, count the failure, and switch to fixed delay so a slow provider never gets a burst of catch-up calls.
steps.code: ScheduledFuture<?> refresher = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { rate = fxProvider.eurUsd(); // 1. fetch lastSuccess = Instant.now(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { failures.increment(); // 2. count it for a metric log.warn("FX refresh failed, keeping {}", rate, e); // 3. keep the old rate } }, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

alt.html: val refresher = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay({ try { rate = fxProvider.eurUsd() // 1. fetch lastSuccess = Instant.now() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { failures.increment() // 2. count it for a metric log.warn("FX refresh failed, keeping {}", rate, e) // 3. keep the old rate } }, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)

steps.say: Make the next failure visible. A health check that reports the rate's age and whether the schedule is still alive turns six silent hours into one alert.
steps.code: boolean healthy = !refresher.isDone() && Duration.between(lastSuccess, Instant.now()).toMinutes() < 5;

alt.html: val healthy = !refresher.isDone && Duration.between(lastSuccess, Instant.now()).toMinutes() < 5

lab.title: Model the timetable, then build a refresher that survives
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail.

Write Schedules.startTimes. Keep the end time of the previous run in a variable. For fixed rate, the start is the later of the due time and that end time; for fixed delay, it is that end time plus the period.
Write SafeTask.wrap: a lambda that runs the task inside a try/catch for RuntimeException and hands the exception to onError.
Write FxRateRefresher: start() calls scheduleWithFixedDelay with an initial delay of 0 and a SafeTask that stores the rate and counts failures; close() cancels the returned future.
Run the tests until all eight pass.
hints: Run 0 of the model always starts at initialDelay, whatever the mode.
Request threads read current() while the scheduler thread writes the rate. Store it in an AtomicReference<BigDecimal> (or a volatile field), not a plain field.
close() must not shut down the scheduler: it belongs to the caller and may run other tasks. Cancel your own ScheduledFuture with cancel(false).

drill.title: A refresher that can't die quietly
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write the code that refreshes a cached value every 10 seconds, measured from the end of each refresh, keeps the old value when a refresh throws, logs the failure, and can be stopped later. Then compare. Which method did you use, and where is the try?

answer.title: Refresh.java
answer.html: ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(); AtomicReference<Limits> limits = new AtomicReference<>(); ScheduledFuture<?> refresh = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { limits.set(loadLimits()); // replace only on success } catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("limit refresh failed, keeping the old value", e); } }, 0, 10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // to stop it refresh.cancel(false); scheduler.shutdown();

alt.title: Refresh.kt
alt.html: val scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor() val limits = AtomicReference<Limits>() val refresh = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay({ try { limits.set(loadLimits()) // replace only on success } catch (e: RuntimeException) { log.warn("limit refresh failed, keeping the old value", e) } }, 0, 10, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // to stop it refresh.cancel(false) scheduler.shutdown()

recap: schedule runs once after a delay, scheduleAtFixedRate follows a timetable, scheduleWithFixedDelay waits a fixed gap after each run ends.
After a slow run, fixed rate starts the overdue runs back to back to catch up. Fixed delay just shifts later runs. Runs of one task never overlap.
If one execution of a periodic task throws, all later executions are suppressed and nothing is logged. Catch RuntimeException inside the task.
ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor is a fixed pool of core threads with an unbounded delay queue; a slow task on one thread delays every other task.
Since JDK 25, ForkJoinPool (including the common pool) implements ScheduledExecutorService and adds submitWithTimeout.
Business schedules belong in a durable scheduler (cron, Quartz with a database, Temporal), not in a pod's memory.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between fixed rate and fixed delay, and why every periodic task in the service needs a try/catch inside it.
explain.answer: Fixed rate keeps a timetable: runs are due at the start time plus multiples of the period, and if a run is slow, the overdue runs start back to back until it's back on schedule. Fixed delay waits the full delay after each run finishes, so a slow run just pushes everything later and nothing bunches up. That makes fixed delay the safer choice for anything that calls a dependency that can slow down. In both modes, if any run throws an exception that escapes the task, the scheduler stops running it forever and logs nothing; the exception sits in the ScheduledFuture that nobody reads. So the task body needs a try/catch that logs the failure and keeps the last good state, and ideally a health check that alerts if the future is done or the last success is too old.

deeper.html:
The clock is System.nanoTime(), not the wall clock. A periodic task is unaffected when NTP corrects the system time or daylight saving time starts, which is what you want for "every 30 seconds". It also means a ScheduledExecutorService can't express "at 02:00 local time". You can approximate it by computing the delay to the next 02:00 and calling schedule again after each run, but that is a sign the job belongs in a real scheduler.

CompletableFuture has its own small scheduling helper, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(delay, unit), which returns an Executor that runs each task after a delay. Lesson 7 of this track uses its relatives, orTimeout and completeOnTimeout.
